Messages.Author: Orpheus
Messages.Body:
Some time ago, I said on this newsgroup that IMO the trouble with the game
was that few masters got played, and that new ones kept coming out. Implying
that a given type of deck would always go round and round on the same old
masters and never get to even risk playing less obvious ones, when you have
Blood Dolls, Directs, Sudden, Dreams... to put in your deck most of the time

Also, there was the problem of playing fatties. If you want them out fast
enough, you need to include quite a few Info Highway and such. But if you
get them in mid to endgame, they are mostly shit.

Then came Anthelios. So, isn't it great ?

Could be. But now we get on another trouble card : Anarch Revolt. If it were
Unique (my long-time proposed "fix"), there would be no problem at all :
without it, I don't see how a deck can win nearly solely with Masters. But
things being what they are, these already very powerful decks become even
more so.

Not to mention that recursion, which we know can be very useful, was until
now limited to the Necromancy discipline (or related minions / object), and
depending on its versions cost an action (except if you became Anarch, which
has a high opportunity cost) at 0 or +1 stealth, and a blood. Giving access
to it to just anyone, although in a limited version (Masters, gotta have one
in hand, costs a master slot) lowers the value of that discipline / Clan I
love.

So, what should we really think of Anthelios, already on top of many
people's Hate List ?

And shouldn't we fix some Masters rather than Anthelios ?

take care of one more pool. But the opportunity cost of playing

I don't care! The difference between the two is *STILL* so stacked
torwards Antedulivian that you can't compare the two! Besides, if
someone *only* loses a minion instead of dying outright, they're
likely to be dead anyway.

I don't disagree that that's a slight advantage for Anarch Revolt.
I just think it's so ridiculously small that it's not worth talking
about. I don't think you can just make Anarch Revolt unique and
call it a night. If you want to make it unique, you have to give
it something back to balance it out. I would propose instead of
making it unique, add the following text:

"Votes to remove the Anarch Revolt begin with two extra votes
lodged against removing it. Anarch Revolt cannot be played if
two Anarch Revolts are already in play."

Instead of making it unique, limit it to two copies. And give it
something back by making harder to remove than just a guy with
the edge or a vote card or something.

> Furthermore, having two different Unique cards offers the
> possibility to put them both in game, which is very different
> from putting only one, wouldn't you agree ?

Nope. It's stupid to have two cards that do the same thing in
a game and have one just be plain BETTER than the other - even
if they're unique. It means that people tend to prefer the one
to the other and throw copies of the good one in first instead
of considering the alternative costs and benefits of each. At
the very least, the good one should be the more common one, if
nothing else (like Bewitching Oration is common and Awe is rare).
The best choice is just to make them of comparable power. I'd
play the Anarch Revolt I proposed. Wouldn't touch yours with
fish wrapping paper.

Fred

I think all of these miss the point. All of these purely weaken a
card that most don't seem to feel is too strong in the first place.
If you weaken a balanced card, you get a weak card. Period.

The other side of the question is that some suggestions people make
(none of the above but I sometimes see them posted) don't even
address the REAL issue most people who complain seem to have with
Anarch Revolt, as I read them: that massed Anarch Revolts is a
brainless strategy which can only be dealt with by the entire board
ganging up to defeat the strategy - and often the player using it
as well - which causes a lot of random things to happen, both in
the execution of the strategy and in its frustration. In short,
few people win consistently with massed Anarch Revolts. But often
they cause the table to collapse randomly which has the effect of
obviating the opponents put into forming their own stratigies.

So an effective, appropriate solution to the problem is not to
just weaken the card and hope it goes away. Not unless you find
wallpapering a card an acceptable solution. Nor is it to just "kind
of" weaken the card and hope to see it used less often. As I
said, that all misses the point. An appropriate solution would be
to find a way to stop it from being used en masse as a strategy but
give it something back to allow players to find other potential
uses for it. Making it unique or otherwise limiting its play
does the former but not latter.

It would be helpful to imagine what an alternate use for it would
be. Orpheus argues that it has use because it's a sure one pool
penalty for one's prey and that's good enough to leave it as is,
unique. I disagree. I think you have to give it some hope to be
useful for something besides that. A simple suggestion would be
to imagine players using it to generally reduce the level of pool
on the table over time but not use it en masse. One of its strengths
in using it en masse was is because the user will put out so many
of them, opponents are challenged to remove them all. If you
just limit the number played in its current state, it's easy as
pie to remove them. Solution: make it harder to remove them as you
limit the number in play at any one time. I gave a proposal to
Orpheus that sounded reasonable to me but I think there are any
number of appropriate choices one could make.

Fred

Well, to each his own opinion, sure. But I think the mass of
experience with collectible card games is that *just* showing that
a card can be neutralized in some way - who cares what way as long
as there's a way - is an insufficient definition of "overpowered".
One of the first, most well-known examples of that was the "black
summer" in the mid '90's when Necropotence decks dominated the
Type II Magic environment. There were decks that could neutralize
Necropotence decks but they were extremely specialized because
Necropotence in that enviroment was so strong that only an extremely
specialized deck could hope to defeat it. Because of this, the
effective environment was reduced to about three archetypes plus a
few very specialized "gadget decks", if I recall correctly.

Refusing to define a card as "overpowered" just because a hose card
for it exists or because one can make an "anti-X deck" is ultimately
a mistake. You have to have a little bit more sophisticated
understanding of games theory to see why, though.

Fred

This is so much untrue that I don't see how it could be written down. ;)

Why on earth would a sane person limit his analysis to the "competent"
opponents? And I'm not even trying to get into that there may be levels
and types of competence, or that competence may be utterly subjective.

In every given tournament, you will face a number of competent and a
number of less than competent players as adversaries. The more competent
players you can trust to make fairer judgements, but the amount of allowed
resources - 30 pool and 90 cards - are the same regardless of competence.
An incompetent player can easily ruin your game, even from cross-table,
because guess what, the guy with two predators _loses_. You must create
your deck in a way that you assume to have one predator - and try to avoid
getting another one, because I hate to say it, but less competent players
are here to stay (unless we forbid anyone from entering the game).

Only the most subtle of deceptions will fool a clever and experienced
player. In fact, in the vast majority of cases the best you can achieve is
to make your adversary guess at the exact odds of you having something
currently available. The less subtle - and often more important -
deception is looking weak to those whose judgement is based more on
superficial impression than on iron-clad experience.

This is a game about vampires. Vampires may appear to be strong or
slender, charming or repulsive, young or old, but their appearance has
little to do with their subtle supernatural powers. Such is fate that a
similarity exists between the players of this game and the characters it
is centered around.

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes

Emmanuel Martin wrote:

> VERY WEAK DECK. I don't see how such a deck can be seen as disruptive.
> OK, it is a weenie bleed deck. And so ? I prefer seating with this

I won't touch what your preferences in predators are, since the other
examples you gave are clearly strong decks, too. But IME, it's easy to
write off weenie bleed deck as not strong mainly due to their being one
of the small handful of decks that will set off the klaxon bells on the
table, after which the rest of the table very smoothly coordinates to
shut them down. So is it weak in a sense? Yes, I agree, but only in a
sense. I would still classify any deck that *needs* the coordinated
effort of the whole table against it as broken, in the sense that it
breaks the game, ie turns it into the pile-on that the pred-prey-VP
mechanic was specifically supposed to deter.

> So congratulations, you have shown that AR can be used in offensive
> decks. OK, but this is precisely the point of AR. However you didn't
> shwo me how it can be abused.

It's the pile on. Pile ons are bad. Dealing tables into omelettes is
sadly common, but also bad. Yes, there is an inescapable subjective
element to the word "bad".

> Your bleed deck doesn't disrupt the table, not more than a rush deck
> (who wants to play with 0 minions ?) or a wall deck (congratulations
> predator, you lost). It just puts a reward on offensive play.

Rush decks have been disruptive in the past. They certainly can still
be disruptive. But I think the disruptiveness was due more in the past
to their slow ousting ability, which lead naturally to needing to
balance tables all over the place and backousting predators. Now, in
theory, there are enough sources of pool damage that their forward
motion could be comparable to other deck types. However, I think they
are *still* just as disruptive despite that, since most preys will just
choose to sit out the game waiting for their rush predator to die, which
in the end is just as disruptive. Bruise-bleed is an answer, but then
it's not really a rush deck. Weenie rush still looks good, but I would
certainly attribute a "bleed something" in their synopsis. Decks that
can fall back on "I bleed you for six with my six nerds" are certainly
not lacking in bleed capability.

As far as walls go, it depends on who is preying on it. The
aforementioned bruise-bleed archetype would probably be tickled to death
with a wall prey. I do agree that decks which rely on stealth or, more
generally, can't handle getting blocked are hosed.

--

David Cherryholmes

one person; the global pool reduction helps the "sputtering out" problem
